interactive.title: The power slosh
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one picture, the power slosh. It is lesson 3's power scrubber with one change: the current wave can now slide. Above, a voltage wave with a 100 V peak and a current wave (dashed, as before) with a 10 A peak share one time axis, 0 to 40 ms, two cycles of a 50 Hz supply; these are the scrubber's example values, so the rms values are 70.7 V and 7.07 A. Drag the current wave left or right, by the small handle on its dashed line or anywhere on the waves, and it slides along the time axis by the phase angle φ, from 90° behind the voltage to 90° ahead of it in steps of 5°, opening at 0°. As in lesson 4, φ is the angle by which the voltage leads the current: positive when the current lags, as a coil's does, and negative when it leads, as a capacitor's does. Below, on the same time axis, is the power wave, voltage × current worked instant by instant, as in lesson 3. Where it is above the line, energy is flowing from the supply into the load, and that area is shaded strongly; where it is below the line, energy is flowing from the load back to the supply, and that area is shaded lightly. A flat dashed line marks the power wave's average, the true power. To the right, the power triangle draws itself from three readouts: true power P along the floor, in watts; reactive power Q upright, in vars, pointing up when the current lags and down when it leads; and apparent power S, the long side, in volt-amps, which is simply V_rms × I_rms, 70.7 × 7.07 = 500 VA, whatever the angle. The rules are P = V I cos φ and Q = V I sin φ, with V and I the rms values, so P² + Q² = S² and the three close a right-angled triangle. Why: the current splits into a part in step with the voltage, I cos φ, and a part a quarter cycle out of step, I sin φ, as Trigonometry lesson 8 split the current arrow into its two shadows. The in-step part times the voltage gives lesson 3's humps, which never dip below the line and average V I cos φ. The quarter-cycle part times the voltage gives lesson 4's slosh, which goes up and down equally and averages zero, with a peak of V I sin φ. The power wave is those two added, so it swings S either side of its average P. Readouts give P, Q and S; the Q readout shows a minus sign when the current leads. Screen 1 opens at φ = 0°, the heater of lesson 3: the power wave is two humps a cycle, all above the line, from 0 to 1000 W, averaging 500 W, with S = 500 VA and Q = 0. The current wave then slides 60° late: the power wave sinks, its top falls to 750 W and its bottom dips to −250 W, so for part of each cycle the voltage and the current have opposite signs and the product is negative. The lightly shaded areas appear below the line, and the dashed average drops to 250 W. Screen 2 holds φ at 60° and asks for the average: 250 W, the middle of a wave that swings from 750 W to −250 W; 500 W (rms volts × rms amps, the resistor's rule); or 375 W (half the 750 W top, lesson 3's rule used where the wave dips). A right Check shows the strongly shaded area above the dashed line matching the gap below it. Screen 3 splits the dashed current wave into two thinner waves that add up to it: the in-step part, with a 10 cos 60° = 5 A peak, and the quarter-cycle part, with a 10 sin 60° = 8.66 A peak. Under each, its own power wave: the in-step part's humps reach 500 W and average 250 W; the quarter-cycle part's slosh swings between 433 W and −433 W and averages 0 W. Added instant by instant they give the power wave above. A row states the rule: the average, with rms values, is P = V I cos φ = 70.7 × 7.07 × 0.5 = 250 W, the true power. Screen 4 returns to lesson 6's bench, 20 V across a 6 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω coil in series, drawing 2 A with the current lagging by 53.13°, and asks for its true power: 24 W, from 20 × 2 × cos 53.13° = 20 × 2 × 0.6; 40 W (volts × amps, the angle left out); or 32 W (the sine used, 20 × 2 × 0.8). A right Check adds the cross-check from the resistor alone: 2² × 6 = 24 W. Screen 5 names the three powers on the triangle at φ = 60°: P = 250 W along the floor, Q = 433 var upright, and S = 500 VA, the long side, with the power factor P ÷ S = 250 ÷ 500 = 0.5, which is cos 60°. Dragging the current wave, the floor and the upright trade length while the long side stays at 500 VA: at 0° the triangle lies flat, P = 500 W and Q = 0; at 90° it stands on end, P = 0 W and Q = 500 var, lesson 4's coil; at −90°, Q = −500 var, lesson 5's capacitor, and the triangle hangs below the floor. Screen 6 is a generator's rating: a 60 Hz diesel set is rated 630 kVA and 504 kW at power factor 0.8, and a load takes 400 kW at power factor 0.6, lagging; how many kVA does it need, and can the set carry it? 667 kVA, no, from S = P ÷ power factor = 400 ÷ 0.6, more than the set's 630 kVA though its 400 kW is inside the 504 kW; 400 kVA, yes (the watts taken for the volt-amps); or 240 kVA, yes (400 × 0.6, multiplying by the power factor where S = P ÷ power factor). The set's 630 kVA is drawn as a dashed arc around the triangle's corner; a right Check draws Q = 533 kvar and S reaching past the arc, and a wrong pick draws its own arc in red. Screen 7 multiplies lesson 6's impedance triangle by the current squared, 2² = 4: R = 6 Ω becomes P = 24 W, X_L = 8 Ω becomes Q = 32 var, and Z = 10 Ω becomes S = 40 VA, so P = I²R, Q = I²X and S = I²Z, and the power triangle has the same 53.13° angle. Each part's own meter gives the same: the resistor's 12 V × 2 A = 24 W, the coil's 16 V × 2 A = 32 var, the supply's 20 V × 2 A = 40 VA. Screen 8 takes lesson 6's screen 6 resistor and coil in series: on 230 V mains they draw 5 A, and the resistor is 40 Ω, so its meter reads 200 V; what is their true power? 1000 W, from 5² × 40, the same as 200 V × 5 A; 756 W (only the in-step part of the current squared, (5 × 0.87)² × 40, where I²R takes the whole current's size); or 1323 W (230² ÷ 40, the whole supply voltage put across the resistance). A right Check draws its triangle: S = 1150 VA, Q = 568 var, power factor 0.87, φ = 29.6°. Screen 9 frees a switch, Hold true power, which fixes P at 500 W. Now dragging the current wave out of step makes it grow taller, because the in-step part must keep its 7.07 A rms, and φ stops at 60° either way, because nearer 90° the current needed for 500 W grows without limit, already 27.3 A rms at 75°. At 60° the current peaks at 20 A, 14.1 A rms, twice the heater's; S grows to 1000 VA and Q to 866 var, while the dashed average stays at 500 W. A cable bar beside the current wave shows the heat in a supply cable of fixed resistance, which goes with the current squared, so at 60° it is 2² = 4 times the heater's. Screen 10 is the course's puzzle: a motor on 230 V draws 10 A while a wattmeter reads 1.6 kW; where has the rest of 2.3 kVA gone? It has not gone anywhere: S = 230 × 10 = 2300 VA, the power factor is 1600 ÷ 2300 = 0.70, and about 1.65 kvar flows out to the motor and back each cycle, so the cable carries all 10 A for 1.6 kW; or 700 W is lost as heat in the motor's windings (heat in the windings is real power, which the wattmeter already counts); or the wattmeter reads low (it reads the average of the power wave, which is all the motor takes). A right Check draws the triangle at φ = 45.9°. Screens 11 and 12 are mixed. Screen 11 slides the current wave 30° ahead of the voltage and asks which is true: P = 433 W and Q = 250 var leading, which the readout shows as −250 var, a power factor of 0.87 leading, with the power wave still dipping to −67 W; P = 250 W (the sine used for the true power); or nothing comes back, because the current leads (a leading current is as far out of step as a lagging one, and the wave dips just the same). Screen 12 takes lesson 7's bench at resonance, 10 V at 50 Hz across 2 Ω, a 10 Ω coil and a 10 Ω capacitor, drawing 5 A, and asks how many vars the supply provides: 0 var, because the coil's 5² × 10 = 250 var lagging and the capacitor's 250 var leading cancel, the two parts handing the energy to and fro between them, so P = 5² × 2 = 50 W, S = 10 V × 5 A = 50 VA and the power factor is 1; 500 var (the two added); or 250 var (the coil's alone); a wrong pick draws its upright in red on the flat triangle. Each puzzle offers three answers; a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, Why? explains in words, and a right Check draws the answer on the picture. The closing line says the energy below the line is not used, only lent and returned, but the current that carries it is real, and that lesson 9 puts a capacitor beside a motor so the motor's vars slosh locally instead of along the supply cable.
interactive.ignores: The waves are pure sines and the supply holds its voltage whatever the load. Dragging φ straight is a shortcut: in a real circuit the angle is set by the load's resistance and reactance, as in lesson 6, and the current's size changes with them. The energy shaded below the line is drawn going back to the supply; on a real installation it goes back towards the supply, and other loads on the same supply may take it on the way. The cable bar shows only the cable's heat, not its voltage drop. A load whose current is not a sine wave, as with many electronic loads, has a power factor that this triangle alone does not give. The circuits and readings are example values.

explain.text:
When a load's current runs out of step with the voltage, the power wave dips below zero for part of every cycle: energy flows out to the load and some of it flows straight back. What the load keeps on average is the true power, in watts. What flows out and back is the reactive power, in vars. Volts times amps is the apparent power, in volt-amps. The three make a right-angled triangle, and the cable and the generator have to carry the current that goes with the long side, not the watts.

Start from lesson 3: the power at each instant is the voltage times the current at that instant. A resistor's voltage and current rise and fall together, so their product never goes below zero, and its power is never returned to the source, as it is with reactive loads.[^3] Now slide the current a phase angle φ behind the voltage, as a coil and a resistor in series do (lesson 6). For part of each cycle the voltage is already positive while the current is still negative, or the other way round, so their product is negative: energy is flowing from the load back to the supply. A coil or a capacitor takes energy in during one part of the cycle and hands it back during another.[^4] To see how much is kept, split the current, as Trigonometry lesson 8 split the current arrow, into a part in step with the voltage, I cos φ, and a part a quarter cycle out of step, I sin φ. The in-step part times the voltage makes lesson 3's humps, which never dip below the line and average V × I cos φ. The quarter-cycle part times the voltage makes lesson 4's slosh, which goes up and down equally and averages nothing. So the average power, with rms values, is P = V I cos φ.[^5] This is the [[true power]], the power actually used, in watts, symbol P.[^6] On the power slosh at 60°, with 70.7 V and 7.07 A, it is 70.7 × 7.07 × 0.5 = 250 W.

The quarter-cycle part still carries energy, out and back twice each cycle. Multiplied by the voltage, it gives lesson 4's slosh, which peaked at 70.7 V × 7.07 A = 500 W with the whole current a quarter cycle out; with only I sin φ of the current out of step, the slosh peaks at V × I sin φ, and that measures how much energy travels. This is the [[reactive power]], Q, in volt-amps reactive, or vars,[^7] 433 var at 60°. Volts times amps with the angle left out, S = V × I, is the [[apparent power]], in volt-amps: 500 VA on the power slosh at any angle, because the current's size does not change as it slides. The two parts of the current are at right angles, so P and Q are the two short sides of a right-angled triangle and S is its long side, with P² + Q² = S². The power factor is P ÷ S, and because P is the side next to φ and S the long side, it equals cos φ:[^8] 0.5 at 60°. On lesson 6's bench the same triangle comes from the circuit: multiply each side of the impedance triangle by the current squared, 2² = 4, and R = 6 Ω gives P = 24 W, all of it heat in the resistor, X_L = 8 Ω gives Q = 32 var, and Z = 10 Ω gives S = 40 VA.

The vars do no work, but the current that carries them is real. Hold the true power at 500 W and open the angle to 60°: only the in-step part of the current, I cos φ, does the work, so it must stay at 7.07 A, and with cos 60° = 0.5 the whole current must be 7.07 ÷ 0.5 = 14.1 A, twice as much; and the heat in the cable, which goes with the current squared, is four times as much. Any power factor less than 1 means the wiring has to carry more current than it would with no reactance.[^9] This is a simplified model, with pure sine waves; a load whose current is not a sine wave has a power factor that this triangle alone does not give. **Out of step, the power wave dips below the line, so the watts used are V I cos φ, the vars sloshing out and back are V I sin φ, and the volt-amps supplied are V × I: the three form a right-angled triangle, and the power factor, P ÷ S, is cos φ.[^8]**

analogy.text: A tug tows a barge with its line at an angle to the barge's track. Only the part of the pull along the track moves the barge; the sideways part does nothing useful, yet the line and its winch must take the whole pull. The pull along the track is the true power, the sideways pull is the reactive power, and the tension in the line is the apparent power. Swing the line out wider and, for the same forward pull, the line's tension grows, as the current grows when the power factor falls.
analogy.breaks: The sideways pull on the line is a steady force that moves nothing, while reactive power is energy really travelling: out to the coil's field or the capacitor's plates and back to the supply, twice every cycle. And a towline's angle stays put, where in a circuit the angle is the time between the current's peak and the voltage's.

practice.text:
- Safety first: a wattmeter and a clamp meter are read on a live circuit, so use kit rated for the circuit and your usual safe working practice.
- Read the rms voltage, the rms current and the wattmeter. The wattmeter gives the true power, P, in watts.
- Apparent power: S = V × I, in volt-amps.
- Power factor: P ÷ S, which is cos φ.[^8] The angle is the one whose cosine that is.
- Reactive power: Q = √(S² − P²), in vars. Square, subtract, square root; never take P from S as plain numbers.
- From a circuit instead: P = I²R, Q = I²X and S = I²Z, using each part's size, not any part of the current.
- At a given voltage, the current, and so the cable's heat, follows S, not P.[^9]

**Rule of thumb:** Watts pay for the work; volt-amps size the kit. A cable or a breaker follows the current, so at a given voltage check it against S, not P. A generator is rated in kVA at a stated power factor,[^10] with a kW figure as well: 100 kVA supplies 80 kW at 0.8,[^11] and a 60 Hz diesel set reads 630 kVA and 504 kW at 0.8.[^12] Check a load against both.

**Worked example:** A motor on 230 V mains[^1] draws 10 A and a wattmeter reads 1.6 kW. S = 230 × 10 = 2300 VA. The power factor is 1600 ÷ 2300 = 0.70, lagging, so φ = 45.9°. Q = √(2300² − 1600²) ≈ 1652 var, about 1.65 kvar, flowing out to the motor's windings and back each cycle. Nothing is missing: the motor takes 1.6 kW, and the cable carries all 10 A to deliver it. The rules are the same on a ship's 60 Hz supply,[^2] because none of the steps from meter readings depends on the frequency.

Lesson 9 puts a capacitor beside such a motor, so its vars slosh between the two locally instead of along the supply cable.

**Common mistakes**
- Calling volts × amps watts. That is S, in volt-amps; P is smaller unless the power factor is 1.
- Taking the gap between S and P as power lost as heat. Heat is true power, and the wattmeter already counts it.
- Working V² ÷ R with the whole supply voltage. Only the resistor's own voltage goes in, or use I²R.
- Taking P from S as plain numbers to find Q. The three make a right-angled triangle.
- Using sin φ for the power factor. It is cos φ, the side next to the angle over the long side.
- Thinking a leading current returns nothing. It is out of step the other way, and its power wave dips just the same.

sources.title: Lessons In Electric Circuits -- Volume II (AC) - Chapter 11
sources.quote: The actual amount of power being used, or dissipated, in a circuit is called true power , and it is measured in watts (symbolized by the capital letter P, as always).

sources.title: Lessons In Electric Circuits -- Volume II (AC) - Chapter 11
sources.quote: This “phantom power” is called reactive power , and it is measured in a unit called Volt-Amps-Reactive (VAR), rather than watts. The mathematical symbol for reactive power is (unfortunately) the capital letter Q.

sources.title: Lessons In Electric Circuits -- Volume II (AC) - Chapter 11
sources.quote: Because true power and apparent power form the adjacent and hypotenuse sides of a right triangle, respectively, the power factor ratio is also equal to the cosine of that phase angle.

sources.quote: lagging power factor loads tend to demagnetize the field and terminal voltage is maintained only by increasing the d.c. field current. Therefore, a.c. generators are rated in terms of load current and voltage output, or kilovolt-ampere (kVA) output, at a specified frequency and power factor.
